FOREWORD 
 
NABARD undertakes annual credit planning exercise, starting with preparation of Potential 
Linked Credit Plans (PLPs) for each district. The process involves multi-level consultation with 
all the stakeholders and convergence of programmes implemented by Sta te Government, 
Central Government, Bankers etc. The State Focus Paper (SFP) is a consolidation of such 
exploitable district level potential as identified in the respective PLPs. The document 
quantifies potential both in physical and financial terms and estimation of bank credit segment 
to actualise the potential.  
The State Focus Paper also highlights various policy/ programme framework of state and 
central governments and suggest refinements, new frameworks and infrastructure required 
for smooth offtake of bank credit in the State of Tamil Nadu. It gives me immense pleasure to 
present the State Focus Paper for 2025-26 which projects a total credit potential of ₹9,37,629 
crore for Priority Sector activities as defined by the Reserve Bank of India. This estimate 
encompasses ₹4,34,583 crore for agriculture, ₹3,45,245 crore for MSME and ₹1,57,801 crore 
for other priority sectors. 
Overall, priority sector lending has been playing a crucial role in promoting economic growth 
and development in Tamil Nadu particularly in Agriculture and MSME. Addressing 
infrastructure and input issues, risk mitigation through insurance schemes, adequat e 
marketing and storage infrastructure and above all Irrigation infrastructure are factors that 
are key for development of the State in future. Despite Tamil Nadu’s extensive irrigation 
infrastructure, inadequate water storage capacity, aging infrastructure, lack of modernisation, 
climate impacts etc. are areas of concern that need attention. Further for growth of MSME, 
initiatives for improving Digital infrastructure, easy access to credit, vocational training and 
education, industry- academia partnerships, access to technology and innovation, Business 
incubators and accelerators are required. The State Focus Paper has delved into the above 
aspects and has come out with suggestions/measures for improvement. 
I place on record my gratitude to State Government, Line Departments, RBI, SLBC, Bankers, 
District Collectors, LDM, NGOs, farmers and other stakeholders for their valuable inputs in 
preparation of this document and wholehearted support to NABARD in our end eavour. We 
welcome suggestions for further augmenting the document on an ongoing basis. 
 
 
 
R Anand 
Chief General Manager

प्रस्तािना 
नाबार्ड प्रत्येक जिले के जलए संभाव्यता युक्त ऋण  योिना (पीएलपी) की तैयारी के साथ ही  वाजषडक 
ऋण आयोिना बनाता है. इस प्रजिया में सभी जहतधारकों के साथ बहु-स्तरीय परामर्ड और राज्य सरकार , 
क ें द्र सरकार , बैंकरों आजि द्वारा कायाडन्वित कायडिमों का अजभसरण र्ाजमल होता है. राज्य फोकस पेपर 
(एसएफपी) संबंजधत पीएलपी में पहचानी गई ऐसी िोहन योग्य जिला स्तरीय क्षमता का समेकन है. यह 
िस्तावेज़ भौजतक और जवत्तीय िोनों दृजि से क्षमता का आकलन करता है और क्षमता को वास्तजवक 
बनाने के जलए बैंक ऋण खंर् का अनुमान लगाता है. राज्य फोकस पेपर राज्य और क ें द्र सरकारों  के 
जवजभन्न प्राथजमकता/कायडिम  ढांचे पर भी प्रकार् र्ालता है और  तजमलनार् ु राज्य में बैंक ऋण के सुचारू  
प्रान्वि के जलए आवश्यक पररर्ोधन, नए ढांचे और बुजनयािी ढांचे का सुझाव भी िेता है। मुझे 2025-26 
के जलए राज्य फोकस पेपर पेर् करते हुए बहुत खुर्ी हो रही है िो भारतीय ररज़वड बैंक द्वारा पररभाजषत 
प्राथजमकता क्षेत्र की गजतजवजधयों के जलए ₹9,37,629 करोड़ की क ु ल ऋण क्षमता का अनुमान लगाता है। 
इस अनुमान में क ृ जष के जलए ₹4,34,583 करोड़, एमएसएमई के जलए ₹3,45,245 करोड़ और अन्य 
प्राथजमकता वाले क्षेत्रों के जलए ₹1,57,801 करोड़ र्ाजमल हैं. 
क ु ल जमलाकर , प्राथजमकता ऋणीकरण क्षेत्र तजमलनार् ु में जवर्ेष रूप  से क ृ जष और एमएसएमई में आजथडक 
वृन्वि और जवकास को बढावा िेने में महत्वपूणड भूजमका जनभा रहा है. बुजनयािी ढांचे और इनपुट मुद्ों 
का जनवारण , बीमा योिनाओं के माध्यम से िोन्वखम को कम करना , पयाडि  जवपणन और भंर्ारण बुजनयािी 
ढांचा और सबसे बढकर जसंचाई बुजनयािी ढांचा ऐसे कारक हैं िो भजवष्य में राज्य के जवकास के जलए 
अजत महत्वपूणड हैं. तजमलनार् ु के व्यापक जसंचाई बुजनयािी ढांचे के बाविूि , अपयाडि  िल भंर्ारण क्षमता, 
पुराना बुजनयािी ढांचा, आधुजनकीकरण की कमी, िलवायु प्रभाव आजि जचंता के क्षेत्र हैं जिन पर जवर्ेष 
ध्यान िेने की आवश्यकता है. इसक े अलावा, एमएसएमई के जवकास के जलए जर्जिटल बुजनयािी ढांचे में 
सुधार , ऋण तक आसान पहुंच, व्यावसाजयक प्रजर्क्षण और जर्क्षा, उद्योग- र्ैक्षजणक भागीिारी , प्रौद्योजगकी 
और नवाचार तक पहुंच, जबिनेस इनक्यूबेटर और एक्सेलेर े टर के पहल की आवश्यकता है. राज्य फोकस 
पेपर ने उपरोक्त पहलुओं पर गहराई से जवचार जकया है और सुधार के जलए सुझाव/उपाय प्रस्तुत जकए 
हैं. 
इसी संिभड में, मैं राज्य सरकार , संबन्वित जवभागों, भारतीय ररिवड  बैंक, एसएलबीसी, बैंकसड, जिला कलेक्टरों, 
एलर्ीएम, एनिीओ , जकसानों और अन्य जहतधारकों के प्रजत आभार व्यक्त करता हं जिन्ोंने इस िस्तावेि 
को तैयार करने में महत्वपूणड योगिान  और नाबार्ड को हमार े प्रयास में जिल से सहयोग जिया है. हम 
इस िस्तावेि को आगे बढाने के जलए जनर ं तर आपक े सुझावों का स्वागत करते हैं.

NABARD as a Development Financial Institution, plays a crucial role in credit planning for 
Agriculture and rural sector for all States in India, through preparation of district wise 
potential linked credit plan under Priority Sector for the banking system,  including Rural 
Financial Institutions (RFIs), on annual basis.  The potential linked credit plans (PLPs) of all 
districts are thereafter aggregated to arrive at the total credit potential for the State, which is 
discussed in detail in the State Focus Pap er. Assessment of credit potential is done through 
analysis of sector specific physical potential, infrastructure support, past credit trends, future 
planned developments, credit absorption capacity, government priorities through various 
schemes, available forward and backward linkages, local skills and natural resources. 
This document serves as a useful reference to provide pointed focus on the development of 
priority sectors of the State with institutional credit support. 
Total geographical area of Tamil Nadu is 130.33 lakh hectare which constitutes 4% of the 
National geographical area and falls in Semi and Dry sub humid climate. Tamil Nadu has 6% 
of the Nation’s population (2011 Census). As per 10th Agriculture Census, 2015-16, the number 
of operational land holders in the State is 79.38 lakh, with operating culturable land of 59.71 
lakh Ha. 93% of total land holdings are Marginal and Small farmers, operating 62% of the total 
cultivable land. The average size of the land ho lding in the State is 0.75 hectare which is less 
than the average size of land holding of the country at 1.08 hectare. 
 
Tamil Nadu is the most progressive state in India in terms of many economic and social 
parameters. It is the second largest economy (₹24.27 lakh crore in 2023 -24) in the country, 
with an ambitious target of achieving a trillion -dollar economy by 2030. Tamil Nadu’s Gross 
State Domestic Product (GSDP) grew 8.13% in 2022 -23 and 8.23% in 2023 -24 at constant 
prices, while at current prices, the growth rates were 15.48% in 2022-23 and 13.71% in 2023-
24. The growth rates for the All India GDP was 6.99% in 2022 -23 and 8.15% in 2023 -24 at 
constant prices, while at current prices, they were 14.21% in 2022 -23 and 9.60% in 2023-24. 
In 2023 -24, the services sector contributed 53% to the state's economy, followed by 
manufacturing at 34% and agriculture at 13%. The service s sector grew at 9.4% in 2023 -24, 
followed by manufacturing at 7.1% and agriculture at 4.3%. 
 
There were 13528 bank branches in Tamil Nadu as on 31 March 2024, comprising of 3607 
branches in rural areas, 4943 in semi -urban and 4977 in urban areas, with 6338 branches of 
Public Sector Banks, 4639 of Private Sector Banks, 663 of Regional Rural Bank, 979 0f Tamil 
Nadu State Apex Co-operative Bank, TNSCARDB and DCCBs, 863 of Small Finance Banks, 11

The Co-operative Credit Structure in the State consists of Short Term and Long Term. The Short Term 
structure has three-tiers, with the Tamil Nadu State Apex Co-operative Bank Ltd (TNStCB) at the apex 
level with 51 branches, 23 District Central Co-operative Banks (DCCBs) at district level with 927 
branches, and 4454 PACS.  Co-operative Banks have 978 branches , comprising of 297 rural 
branches, 269 Semi-urban branches, 412 urban & Metro. TNStCB and all the 23 DCCBs are on 
CBS platform. PACS computerization is being implemented under the GoI project, covering 4532 Co-
operative Societies including all the 4,453 PACS and the same is expected to be completed by 31 March 
2025. This will facilitate general public in a larger way besides strengthening the functioning of PACS 
and to have effective monitoring. 
The Long -Term Co -operative Credit structure consists of Tamil Nadu State Co -operative 
Agricultural and Rural Development Bank (TNSCARDB) and 80 Primary Co -operative 
Agricultural and Rural Development Bank (PCARDB).  
 
This scheme aims at computerization of all functional ACS leading to increase in efficiency, 
profitability, transparency and accountability.   All the 4532 cooperative societies have been 
covered under the CSPCP project for bringing all the functional societies onto a common 
software, linking them with NABARD through State Cooperative Bank (StCB) and District 
Central Cooperative Banks which is implemented by NABARD. 
 
The target fixed under ACP for the FY’24 was ₹ 700420 crore as against which disbursement 
was ₹ 663993 crore registering an achievement of 94.8% and 24.73% growth from previous 
year. Total Agriculture Credit during FY 2023-24 was Rs.404334cr registering an achievement 
of 105%.  As on 31 March 2024, CD ratio for all financial institution stood at 121% which is 
higher than the previous FY (113%).  
 
Agriculture is the livelihood for around 45% of the rural population in Tamil Nadu. Major food 
crops grown in the State are rice, jowar, ragi, bajra, maize, pulses and oil seeds like 
groundnuts, sesame, and sunflower. Few other crops that are cultivated extensively are cotton, 
sugarcane, tea, coffee, and coconut.  Paddy is the leading crop and is grown in all the seasons 
i.e., Kuruvai, Samba and Kodai. The production of food grains during the year 2023 -24 was 
118.02 lakh MT (as per Third Advance Estimate, 2 023-24) amidst natural calamities like

deficit rainfall during south-west monsoon, crop damage due to cyclone in northern districts 
and extremely heavy rainfall in southern districts during December 2024.  Tamil Nadu is one 
of the leading Horticulture States in the country contributing 6.09% of national horticulture 
production and 5.47% of total horticulture crops in terms of area at national level. Rapid 
growth of demand for horticulture commodities and pro ducts have resulted in shift or 
diversification from traditional food crops to horticulture crops like banana, coconut, mango, 
vegetables, medicinal / herbal / aromatic plants etc.  
 
For the fourth successive year, an exclusive Agriculture Budget 2024-25 for the State of Tamil 
Nadu was presented keeping in line the Government’s priority for the Agriculture sector. 
Focus of the Agriculture Budget 2023 -24 is on crop diversification, floo d protection, water 
conservation and farmer welfare Schemes. Agriculture Budget for 2024 -25 increased the 
allocation for agriculture and allied sectors to ₹42,281.88cr, i.e. 8.7% higher than the 
₹38,904 Cr in the Budget estimate for 2023-24.  
 
 
In rural areas of Tamil Nadu, major infrastructure gaps identified are in irrigation, roads and 
bridges, power supply, education, skilling etc. NABARD has been partnering with Government 
of Tamil Nadu for filling these gaps by extending support for creatio n of infrastructure in 
Agriculture, Social and Rural Connectivity Sectors through various funds like RIDF, WIF, 
NIDA, CFF, LTIF, MIF, DIDF and FIDF. NABARD funded 47295 projects to the tune of  
₹37902.04 Cr for creation of rural infrastructure. Of this, an amount of ₹31719.22 crore has 
been disbursed as on 31.12.2024. Investments under RIDF, in turn, have helped NABARD to 
fulfil the mandate by improving the credit absorption capacity, increased access to markets, 
enhanced incomes and better quality of life in rural Tamil Nadu. Currently, assistance from 
RIDF is available for supporting 39 eligible activities grouped under three distinct heads viz. 
Agriculture and related sectors, Social Sectors and Rural Connectivity. 
NABARD Infrastructure Development Assistance (NIDA), is a line of credit for funding rural 
infrastructure projects for funding rural infrastructure projects directly to State Government 
and State -owned Institutions under 16 eligible activities. NABARD, so far has extended 
₹6767.23 crore to State Government and State-owned Institutions under various activities. 
Fisheries & Aquaculture Infrastructure Development Fund (FIDF), is implemented through 
NABARD to fund the public infrastructure components to State Governments/Union 
Territories for various fishery -based infrastructure activities. As on date, NABARD has 
extended ₹1314.73 crore to State Government. 
Credit Facility for Federations (CFF) is extended with objective of providing short-term loans 
to State Marketing /Co-operative federations and Corporations involved in procurement and 
marketing of Agricultural commodities and supply of agricultural inputs . NABARD, has 
extended ₹17,500 crore to various State Govt Corporations.

Warehouse Infrastructure Fund (WIF), a dedicated fund of Govt. of India implemented 
through NABARD, aims for extending financial assistance to public and private players in the 
warehousing sector for eligible activities. As on date, NABARD has extended  ₹2636.60 crore 
to State Government. 
Food Processing Fund (FPF), a fund constituted by Govt. of India in NABARD for promotion 
of food processing industry in the organised sector on a cluster basis by providing affordable 
credit for setting up of designated food parks notified by Ministry of food Processing industries 
(MOFPI), GoI and establishing food processing units therein. As on date NABARD has 
extended ₹439.79 crore to various stakeholders in Tamil Nadu for establishment of food 
parks. 
Further, NABARD, has extended ₹1357.93 crore and ₹549 crore under Micro Irrigation Fund 
(MIF) and Dairy processing & Infrastructure Development Fund (DIDF) respectively. 
 
NABARD has been extending grant assistance to Banks for almost a decade and a half for 
putting in place the required financial inclusion infrastructure, as well as for providing 
financial literacy. Despite the best efforts put in by all the stakeholders, there exist disparities 
in terms of financial exclusion and in -adequacy of technology adoption. Therefore, a 
differentiated strategy has been adopted from the year 2019 -20 for extending support under 
FIF, to provide more thrust on backward districts and technologically weak banks, to deepen 
the efforts of financial inclusion for the benefit of hitherto excluded population.  
The Rural Cooperative Banks (RCBs) and RRBs in the State are guided by NABARD for on -
boarding to technology solutions including regulatory requirements. The RCBs and the RRBs 
in the State have been extended grant assistance for on -boarding to Public Financ e 
Management System (PFMS) portal of Government of India, Bharat Bill Payment System, 
Positive Pay System and implementation of BHIM-UPI in Banks. Banks have been supported 
to the tune of ₹70 lakh for various technological interventions. 
To expand digital payment infrastructure in rural areas, NABARD is extending financial 
support to all banks (Scheduled Commercial Banks/Small Finance Banks/Payment 
Banks/RRBs/Cooperatives) for deployment of PoS/m -PoS devices in tier 3 to 6 centres. All 
Banks are being encouraged to deploy micro-ATMs in Schools/ colleges/milk societies /fixed 
BC points/Branches/PACSs and other non -credit societies. During the past FY, Banks have 
been sanctioned grant support to the extent of ₹25 lakh and ₹426.35 lakh from NA BARD for 
deployment of PoS devices and micro-ATMs in the State respectively.  
 
With a view to catering to the demand side of the FI initiative, there is a need for spreading 
financial and digital literacy among the rural population. 64 Centers for Financial Literacy 
covering 192 blocks were set up by four Lead Banks (Indian Overseas Bank-20, Indian Bank -
22, Canara Bank -16 and State Bank of India –6) with grant assistance of ₹1875.2 lakh from 
NABARD.  
In order to achieve a meaningful and comprehensive Financial Inclusion and to ensure 
financial security to the poor and the vulnerable, especially in Special Focus Districts in the

State, NABARD has sanctioned grant support of ₹89.75 lakh to various Banks towards conduct 
of around 1800 Financial & Digital Literacy Awareness Programmes across the State. 
 
NABARD has been partnering with Tamil Nadu Watershed Development Agency 
(TAWDEVA), CSR funds and NGOs for implementation of watershed projects. So far 203 
watershed projects have been sanctioned in 28 districts covering 2.19 lakh ha. in the State with 
a cumulative grant support of ₹183.28 crore. Out of these 203 projects, 141 are implemented 
in partnership with the GoTN, 41 under full grant by NABARD through NGOs and 21 projects 
under CSR partnership mode. Climate Proofing activities are being implemented i n 30 
completed Watershed projects in 09 districts with grant assistance of ₹15 crore. 
NABARD in collaboration with KfW is Implementing SEWOH Phase III programme (KfW  
Soil Project) on ‘Integration of Watershed Development for rehabilitation of degraded soil and 
climate change adaptation’ to reduce vulnerability to climate change by the stabilization, 
enhancement and sustainable use of soil and water resources. NABARD TNRO has sanctioned 
25 KfW Soil projects in 14 districts with grant support of Rs.15.42 crore, to 13 Project 
facilitating agencies (PFAs) covering beneficiaries of small and marginal farmers.  Under this 
KfW Soil project, the various components sanctioned a re additional SWC measures, Soil 
Health improvement and productivity enhancement measures, Promotion of sustainable NRM, 
CCA farming practices and Food security, Measures to Mitigate CC risk and Capacity building, 
institutional building and knowledge management.  
 
NABARD has sanctioned 30 Tribal Development Fund (TDF) Projects with grant support of 
₹75.18 crore, to various Project Implementing Agencies (PIAs) covering beneficiaries from 
15108 families . Under these TDF projects, various activities like support for horticulture 
orchard / plantation in one or half acre wadi area, water resources Development & Soil 
Conservation activities, livelihood activities for landless families, capacity building/awareness 
programs/training programs etc., Community health and women development are being 
undertaken.  
 
Tamil Nadu is having a conducive ecosystem for formation and nurturing of FPOs. There are 
around 1200 FPOs in the State, of which 476 have been promoted by NABARD and around 
386 with the support of TNSFAC through TN State Government and the remaining by various 
other agencies apart from few self -promoted FPOs. Initiatives of NABARD include grant 
support to FPOs, with total grant of ₹94,28 crore, capacity building, market facilitation, 
establishment of NABKISAN for financing FPOs, establishment of three incubation centres for 
providing business services for FPOs (Tamil Nadu) and supporting GoI scheme of promotion 
of 10,000 FPOs.

Aggregating producers into Clusters/OFPOs is one best mechanisms to improve access of 
small producers in off-farm sector to investment, technology and market. NABARD has been 
promoting the formation and nurturing of Off Farm Producer Organizations since 2016-17. 
NABARD, TN RO as on 31 December 2024, has sanctioned grant assistance to the tune of 
₹186.38 lakh for formation and nurturing of 04 major OFPOs in Tamil Nadu aggregating 
over 1500 producers. 
 
With the growing unemployment amongst rural youth and asymmetrical development of skill-
based employment opportunities concentrated in Metros, Urban and semi urban areas, there 
is a wide gap between the demand for skilled job and rural youth to be imparted  skilling, 
reskilling and up- skilling through capacity building/training.  NABARD addresses the issue 
through its skill development programme 32 Skill development programmes for providing 
training to 925 rural youth were supported with total financial sanction of ₹160.55 lakh during 
2023-24. The 20 agencies supported included ETIs, NGOs and CSR partners. An amount of ₹ 
148.24 lakh was disbursed in 2023 -24 and ₹71 lakh was disbursed in 2024 -25 (up to 
31.12.2024) for Skill development programmes. 
 
Under Rural Mart scheme of NABARD assistance is provided to producers/artisans/weavers 
for setting up shops in a prominent location on a highway, religious place, place of tourist 
importance, thoroughfare where a number of people pass through, for selling locally made 
products. Under the scheme grant assistance of ₹239.26  lakh has been extended to 60 Rural 
Marts and Mobile Rural Marts upto 31 December 2024.  
A haat or bazaar is an open-air market that serves as a trading venue for local people in rural 
areas. These are periodic markets which normally works on a weekly cycle. Under NABARD’s 
‘Rural Haat’ scheme, cumulatively 13 Rural Haats have been sanctioned t o various agencies 
with a grant assistance of ₹150.66 lakh. 
NABARD has been organizing as well as sponsoring artisans to participate in exhibition 
conducted across the State and Pan India, exhibitions, buyer seller meet and Start -up 
Immersion Program for Agri -Start-ups. These provide effective forward linkage to the rural 
masses for their produce with assured income and employment as also to boost their earning 
capacity. During 2023-24, grant support of ₹ 31.32 lakh has been provided to various artisans 
and an amount of ₹ 40.61 lakh has been extend during 2024 -25 (31 .12.2024) under this 
scheme.

As of March 2024, SHGs in TN reported a savings balance of ₹2854.39 crore and credit

shattered myths about the “non-bankability” of the poor. However, the state’s SHG NPAs are 
at 6.67%, much higher than the national average of 2.05%. NABARD’s capacity -building 
initiatives aim to address this concern. 
 
NABARD supports SHG skill -building via the Micro Enterprise Development Programme 
(MEDP) and Livelihood and Enterprise Development Programme (LEDP), offering training 
in diverse fields like food processing, embroidery, livestock farming, and handicrafts. Between 
2018 and 2024, 290 MEDPs were sanctioned w ith NABARD assistance of ₹242.9 lakhs.

2024. The My Pad -My Right (MPMR) initiative in collaboration with NABFOUNDATION 
promotes sanitary pad production through SHGs, enh ancing livelihood and menstrual 
hygiene. In TN, it has been launched in Ramanathapuram and Virudhunagar. 
NABARD supports the m-Suwidha scheme, a DPR mode project, to enhance the capacities & 
income levels of SHGs and JLGs by identifying skill gaps and promoting sustainable micro -
enterprises with credit support from banks. The scheme aims to establish at least 500 micro-
enterprises through a cluster approach, facilitating collaboration with sector experts fostering 
economic empowerment for women.

(JLGs) initially for augmenting flow of credit to landless tenant farmers cultivating land for 
crop loan purposes and subsequently to micro entrepreneurs/artisans and others. 
Tamil Nadu is one of the front runner States in JLG nurturing and promotion. As at the end 
of 31 March 2023, 38.66 lakh JLGs were extended bank loan to the tune of ₹13892441.31 lakh 
(source: Status of Microfinance in India 2023-27) 
NABARD has signed MoUs with various scheduled Banks for formation and credit linking of

resources is 750 cubic meters when compared to the national average of 2,200 cubic meters. 
Agriculture is the largest consumer of water in the State using 75 % of the State’s water 
resources. The State is entirely dependent on rains for rechargin g its water resources.

need for mechanization of agricultural operations. Post-harvest machinery also helps in value

damages.

MSMEs of Tamil Nadu are a key contributor to the State’s economy and to Tamil Nadu's vision 
of becoming one Trillion USD economy. With over 25 lakh Udyam registrations, Tamil Nadu 
is the 2 nd  in the country in Udyam registr ations (Ministry of MSMEs, GoI). 26% of Tamil 
Nadu’s entrepreneurs are women which is a testimony to the State’s inclusive growth and 
conducive business environment. 
Tamil Nadu is a leader in Auto parts and components, readymade garments and leather and 
leather goods. The majority of MSMEs in Tamil Nadu are concentrated in sectors such as food 
and beverages, textiles and apparel, printing, metal fabrication, machinery and equipment, 
leather, rubber and plastics, chemicals, wood and furniture etc. Manufacturing MSMEs are 
largely concentrated in Chennai, Coimbatore, Erode, Kanchipuram, Krishnagiri, Madurai, 
Salem, Tiruppur, Virudhunagar and Vellore Districts. Service MSME s are concentrated in 
Chennai, Coimbatore, Dindigul, Kanchipuram, Namakkal, Salem, Thoothukudi, Thiruvallur, 
Trichy and Vellore districts.  
The GoTN has announced many schemes/subsidy shames for MSME sector such as subsidy 
schemes for micro manufacturing enterprises, industrially Backward Blocks and Agro Based 
Enterprises, Special Capital Subsidy for Thrust Sector Enterprises, Generator Subsidy, back -
ended Interest Subsidy.  
Facilitating the creation of a conducive environment for MSMEs to connect with markets and 
ensuring easy access to affordable credit, enabling regulatory environment, simplifying 
administrative processes, and strengthening the credit delivery mechanism hav e been 
outlined in the paper.

garments, textiles, automobiles, agricultural products (such as fruits, rice, and vegetables), 
cotton, oil, turmeric, fireworks, handicrafts, rubber and rubber products, leather and leather 
goods, horticultural products, spices, masala, silk and cotton sarees, and marine products.  
Tamil Nadu is a key exporting State with a share of 10.15% of India’s total exports in 2023-24 
and has been rightly acknowledged as the leading State in the Export Preparedness Index 
compiled by the Government of India. The electronics sector witnessed an astounding growth 
with exports touching USD 9.5 billion which is 33% of India’s total exports in this sector. 
Industry-friendly electronics policy, ease of doing business, skilled talent and presence of port 
infrastructure have been key enablers. Likewise,  the State leads in exports of auto & auto 
components, engineering goods, textiles, leather and other principal commodities, with the 
State achieving a whopping USD 44 billion export performance in 2023-24. 
To bolster its export capabilities further, Tamil Nadu has developed four Agri Export Zones 
targeting specific commodities: cut flowers in Hosur (covering Dharmapuri and Krishnagiri), 
flowers in Nilgiris District, mangoes in Theni (including Dindigul and M adurai), and cashew 
nuts in Cuddalore (covering Thanjavur and Pudukkottai).

1.1. Introduction: Tamil Nadu is the tenth largest State in the country with a geographical 
area of 1,30,058 Sq.km. The state shares about 4.11 % of the country’s total geographical area 
and has a coastline of 1076 km. It is located in the Indian Peninsula between Bay of Bengal in 
the east , the Indian Ocean in the south and sharing borders with the Union Territory of 
Puducherry and Southern Indian States of Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka on the north and 
Kerala on the west. The State has 38 districts, 87 Revenue Divisions, 310 Taluks, 1349 Firkas, 
17680 Revenue Villages, 15 Municipal corporations, 121 Municipalities, 385 Panchayat Unions 
(Blocks), 490 Town Panchayats, 12525 Village Panchayats, 39 Lok Sabha Constituencies and 
234 Assembly Constituencies.  
1.2 Agro -climatic zones : Based on rainfall, soil characteristics, cropping pattern and 
irrigation potential, the State has  been divided into  seven distinct agro -climatic zones, viz., 
North Eastern, North Western, Western, Cauvery Delta, Southern, High Rainfall and Hill and 
high altitude Zones. All the districts under Cauvery Delta were declared as Protected Special 
Agricultural Zone by GoTN. There are four seasons in the State viz., Southwest Monsoon (June 
to September), Northeast monsoon (October to December), winter (January to February) and 
hot weather (March to May).  
1.3 Rainfall: The State's average  annual rainfall is around 99 0 mm which is less t han the 
National average of 1,257 mm. The quantum of rainfall received is 39% during the Northeast 
monsoon, 42% during the southwest monsoon, 11% during summer, and 8% during winter. 
The total surface water  potential of the State is 865 TMC , which includes 260 TMC realized 
from the neighboring States through Inter-State Agreements.  
 (Source: Statistical Handbook of Tamil Nadu 2021-22, Department of Economics & Statistics, GoTN) 
1.4 Population:  Tamil Nadu is the s eventh most populated state in the country with a 
population density of 555 persons per sq. km. against the national average of 382 (as per 2011 
Census). The state shares about 6% of the country’s total population.  The total population is 
7.21 crore out of which the male population is 3.61 crore and female population is 3.60 crore. 
The rural population is 3.72 crore forming 51.60% of the total population and the urban 
population is 3.49 crore forming 48.40% of the total p opulation. The state's literacy rate was 
80.09% in 2021, which is above the national average of 77.7% with male literacy at 82.04% 
and female literacy at 64.55%.  
(Source: https://tnenvis.nic.in/Database/Demography) 
1.5 Pattern of Land Holding:  As per the 10 th Agricultural Census, Tamil Nadu has 79.38 
lakh landholders cultivating an area of 59.71 lakh ha. 93% of total land holdings are owned by 
Marginal and Small farmers, operating 62 % of the total cultivable lands. The remaining 7% 
are medium and large farmers accounting for 38% of the total cultivable lands. The  average 
land holding size of Tamil Nadu is 0.75 ha, which is less than the national average of 1.08 ha.  
 (Source: Policy Note 2024-25, Agriculture and Farmers Welfare Department)

The principal food crops of the State include paddy, jowar, ragi, bajra, maize, other millets and 
pulses. Horticulture crops such as mango, banana, tomato, cucurbits  and commercial crops 
such as sugarcane, cotton, sunflower, coconut, cashew, chillies, gingelly and groundnut  are 
also extensively grown in Tamil Nadu . Major p lantation crops grown are  tea, coffee, 
cardamom and rubber. Major forest produces are timber, sandalwood, pulp wood and fuel 
wood. Paddy is the leading crop and is grown in all 3 seasons’ viz. Kuruvai (Apr-Jul), Samba 
(Aug-Nov) and Kodai (Dec-Mar). Tamil Nadu has also gained a commendable status in cash 
and oilseed crops viz., groundnuts, sesame, sunflower, etc.  Food grain production fell to 107.00 
lakh metric tonne during the year 2023-24, against 116.80 lakh metric tonne achieved during the 
year 2022-2023. Tamil Nadu is poised to achieve 129.63 lakh metric tonne of food grain production 
in 2024-25.  
(Source: Policy Note 2024-25 Agriculture and Farmers Welfare Department)  
1.9 Horticulture: Tamil Nadu is one among the leading horticulture States in India, contributing 
6.09% of production with 5.47% of area at national level. In Tamil Nadu, horticulture crops are 
cultivated in an area of 16.03 lakh ha., with a total production of 233.9 lakh MT.  Area cultivated 
under fruit crops during 2022-23 was 3.34 lakh ha. Mango and banana are the main fruit crops.  
Vegetable crops and plantation crops are cultivated in an area of 3.62 lakh ha. and 7.33 lakh 
ha. respectively. The climatic conditions prevailing in Tamil Nadu is favourable for growing flowers 
like jasmine (malligai, mullai, pitchi and kakada), tuberose (sambangi), crossandra, chrysanthemum, 
rose, marigold, nerium, etc. 27% of the total flower area cultivated is Jasminum sp. (gundu malligai, 
mullai, pitchi and kakada) followed by Chrysanthemum (Samanthi), which shares 20% of the area

State Value Added (GSVA) and 43.70% to agriculture and allied activities.  Tamil Nadu has 
9.52 million cattle, 0.52 million buffaloes, 4.50 million sheep, 9.89 million goats, 0.07 million 
pigs and 120.78 million poultry sharing a considerable proportion to national livestock wealth. 
The State ranks 1st in respect of poultry, 4th in sheep, 7th in goat, 13th in cattle and 14th in buffalo 
population in the country. Tamil Nadu has 245 lakh of livestock and 1207.80 lakh poultry 
(2019 census). 
The milk production in Tamil Nadu in 2023-24 has increased by 6.93% as compared to 2022-
23. The per capita availability of milk in India increased to 471 gram per day in 2023-24 from 
459 gram per day in 2022-23. In Tamil Nadu, the per capita availability of milk has increased 
from 369 grams per day in 20 22-23 to 3 84 grams per day during 202 3-24. (Basic Animal 
Husbandry Statistics 2024, MoFAHD, GoI) 
1.11 Fisheries : Tamil Nadu is enriched with diverse, abundant and productive brackish, 
marine and inland fisheries resources, providing the fisheries sector an important role in 
maintaining prosperity of the state.  The state has 14 coastal districts with an Exclusive 
Economic Zone of 1.9 lakh sq. km and a continental shelf of 41,412 sq.km. The State has 608 
fishing villages, and the fisheries sector supports livelihood of more than 10.48 lakh marine 
fisher folk. 
Tamil Nadu has 1,076 km long coastline, which is the 2 nd largest in the country. Marine fish 
production of the State during 2022-23 was 8.29 lakh Tonnes, of which 1. 23 lakh Tonnes, 
valued at ₹6,957.67 crore has been exported. The inland fisheries sector supports the 
livelihood of 2.36 lakh inland fisherfolk of the State. An estimated brackish water area of 
56,000 ha is available in the form of lagoons, estuaries and back waters, which are potential 
source of capture fisheries. There are 2 360 farms spread ov er an area of 4536.46 ha under 
coastal aquaculture.

1.12 Industry Sector: Tamil Nadu leads the country with the highest number of factories 
at 39672 engaging 15% of persons in India and contributing 10.33% of the gross value 
addition to India’s manufacturing GDP.  
The state ranked 3rd for Gross Value Added(GVA) (₹ 14.44 lakh Cr.), Net Value Added (₹1.93 
lakh Cr.) and 4th for invested capital (₹3.27 lakh Cr.). Tamil Nadu is one of the most efficient 
state economy in terms of net value added to output and high employment generation.  
Tamil Nadu is a manufacturing hub in the country due to its significant presence in sectors 
such as automobiles and auto -components (including Electric Vehicles), textiles & wearing 
apparel, leather, chemicals (including rubber & plastic), electronics, mac hinery, and 
fabricated metal products.The State is home to 130 "Fortune 500” companies such as BMW, 
Hyundai, Daimler, TVS, Renault -Nissan, Citroen, DELL, HP, Samsung, Michelin, MRF, 
Danfoss, Vestas, Hitachi, L&T , Foxconn, Tata  etc. With the launch of the r evised EV Policy 
during February 2023, Tamil Nadu is looking forward to enhance its footprint in the EV sector. 
Companies such as Ola Electric, Ather Energy, Simple Energy, Switch Mobility have a strong 
presence in Tamil Nadu.  
Tamil Nadu is a key exporting state with a share of 10.15% of India’s total exports during 2023-
24 and has been rightly acknowledged as the leading state in the Export preparedness Index 
(EPI) compiled by Government of India. The electronic sector witnessed an astounding growth 
with exports touching US $9.5 billion which is 33% of India’s total exports in this sector. The 
state also leads in exports of auto and auto components, engineering goods, textiles, leather 
and other principal commodities, with the S tate achieving a whopping US $44 billion export 
performance during 2023-24. 
(Source: Industries Department Policy Note 2024-25, ASI Report 2022-23) 
1.13 Renewable Energy : Tamil Nadu is at the forefront of India’s renewable energy (RE) 
transformation with the total installed capacity of Power in Tamil Nadu standing at 41126.68 MW, of 
which, 26% is from Wind, 19.81% is from Solar, 0.50% is from Bio-mass and 1.66 % is from Co-
generation which are renewable sources of energy.  Renewable energy accounts for 48% of total 
installed capacity in the state. TN stood third in total renewable energy installed capacity and fifth in 
renewable energy generation. Tamil Nadu stands 4th in India in solar energy with an installed capacity 
of 8211.38 MW. Tamil Nadu stands 2nd in the installed wind capacity of 10603.54 MW accounting for 
24 percent of the nation’s wind power capacity. Tamil Nadu has the highest off-shore wind energy 
potential with maximum wind speeds ranging from 9 m/s to 11 m/s. 
 (Source: Energy Department Policy Note 2024-25 & GOI Renewable Energy Statistics 2023-24) 
1.14 Service Sector: The state economy is predominantly service sector based with 53.62% 
of Gross State Value Added (GSVA) contributed by this sector. Chennai is the largest software 
exporter in India next to Bangalore. India’s largest IT Park is housed near Chennai. GoTN has 
promoted numerous industrial parks like Rubber Park, Apparel Park, Floriculture Park and 
Agri Export Zones. It is also a hub for e-publishing. Namakkal is a major transport hub of the 
country. Transport, real estate, banking & insuranc e also continue to be major contributors 
under service sector. The sector has been recording impressive growth over the years.

and Salem. Tamil Nadu with a long coastline has 3 major ports at Chennai, Ennore , and

also has Tamil Nadu Agriculture University (TNAU), Tamil Nadu Veterinary and Animal 
Sciences University (TANUVAS) and Tamil Nadu Dr J Jayalalitha Fisher ies University

fishery sectors , respectively. Tamil Nadu has a robust public as well private health 
infrastructure. Good hospitals providing excellent medical facilities attract a large number of 
patients from other parts of the country and world especially for the specialized cancer, dental 
and optical treatment. With advanced medical care available in Chennai, Vellore, Coimbatore, 
and Madurai, Tamil Nadu has become a favored destination of medical tourism.

Tamil Nadu is the most progressive state in India in terms of many economic and social 
parameters. It is the second largest economy (₹27.21 lakh crore in 2023 -24) in the country, 
with an ambitious target of achieving a trillion -dollar economy by 2030 ( Handbook of 
statistics on Indian States 2023 -24, RBI).  It is a highly industrialized state, contributing 
12.25% of the manufacturing real GDP of the country and its share of India's real GDP is 9.08% 
(2022-23). Tamil Nadu ranks first in number of factories and  Export Preparedness Index 
(2022); second in urbanization (53.68%, next only to Kerala), low Infant Mortality Rate (13), 
and low birth rate (13.8) and in head count ratio, i.e., percentage of population who are 
multidimensionally poor (2.2%); third in credit-deposit ratio (in 2022-23) and life expectancy 
at birth, and fourth in literacy and per capita. It is a benchmark state for model startup 
ecosystem, and it is placed in the ‘Best Performer’ category in the States Startup Ranking, 2022 
income (Economic overview of Tamil Nadu 2023-24, MSE). 
Tamil Nadu’s Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) grew 8.13% in 2022 -23 and 8.23% in 
2023-24 at constant prices, while at current prices, the growth rates were 15.48% in 2022-23 
and 13.71% in 2023 -24. The growth rates for the All India GDP were 6.99% in 202 2-23 and 
8.15% in 2023 -24 at constant prices, while at current prices, they were 14.21% in 2022 -23 
and 9.60% in 2023 -24. Tamil Nadu’s inflation rates were 5.97% in 2022 -23 and 5.37% in 
2023-24, compared to the All-India inflation rates of 6.65% and 5.38% during the respective 
periods. 
Tamil Nadu’s average economic growth rate was 5.80% in real terms from 2012 -13 to 2020-
21. The growth rates for 2021 -22, 2022 -23, and 2023 -24 were 7.89%, 8.13%, and 8.23% 
respectively at constant prices. This resulted in an average growth rate of 8.08%, re flecting a 
notable improvement in the State’s overall economic performance compared to earlier years. 
Tamil Nadu’s per capita income was estimated at ₹1,66,590 in 2022 -23 and ₹1,79,732 in 
2023-24, compared to India’s per capita income of ₹99,404 in 2022 -23 and ₹1,06,744 in 
2023-24 at constant prices. Tamil Nadu’s per capita incomes were 1.68 times the national per 
capita income for both years. At current prices, Tamil Nadu’s per capita income was 
₹2,77,802 in 2022 -23 and ₹3,15,220 in 2023 -24, whereas the All -India per capita income 
was ₹1,69,496 in 2022-23 and ₹1,84,205 in 2023 -24. Thus, Tamil Nadu’s per ca pita income 
at current prices was 1.71 times of the national per capita income in 2023-24. (TN Department 
of Economics and Statistics) 
In 2023 -24, the services sector contributed 53% to the state's economy, followed by 
manufacturing at 34% and agriculture at 13%.

Agri Stack is the digital foundation being set up by the government to make it easier to bring 
various stakeholders together to improve agriculture in India and enable better outcomes and 
results for the farmers by using data and digital services. Agri Sta ck is an infrastructure and 
foundational layer that enables various government and private entities to provide farmers 
with tailored services by providing them access to high-quality, validated, attested and current 
data. Agri Stack will provide data to identify genuine farmers (Farmer ID), pinpoint the farm 
location (Farm ID) through geotagging and track what crop is being grown by them through a 
Crop Survey. Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) and standardized protocols defined 
by the Unified Farmer  Service Interface (UFSI) will enable the seamless and standardized 
exchange of information and data with authorized private entities and their digital systems. 
Growers Online Registration of Agriculture Inputs System (GRAINS), a unified farmer’s 
service interface portal of GoTN is aligned with Agri Stack portal of GoI which will be utilized 
for availing all the scheme benefits by the farmers under a single platfo rm. The three core 
registries of the GRAINS consist of Unified Farmer Database, Geo-referencing of land parcels 
in Tamil Nadu and Digital Crop Survey which forms the architecture of the GRAINS portal. 
The GRAINS portal in Tamil Nadu offers a range of services to various stakeholders. By using 
reliable farmer data from the portal, the financial institutions can extend seamless credit and 
other financial services to farmers. It’s a new platform where information on bank accounts, 
Aadhar numbers of landowners and cultivators, land facts, and crop cultivation details would 
be collected and digitised.  
A pilot Digital Crop Survey (DCS) was taken up in 110 villages of the state @ 3 villages per 
district during 2023. DCS has been carried out in all districts of Tamil Nadu through Revenue 
Department. Registration of 54.21 lakh farmers has been completed. La nd parcels of about 
133.62 lakh have been captured. The crop survey has been completed for Kharif season 2024 
and crop survey for Rabi season commenced from 01 November 2024. The data is captured 
using “e-Adangal” application. The “Tamil Nilam” application database maintains the details 
of land record and in turn handles all the transactions relating to Land Records in the State. 
The Tamil Nilam application is interfaced with the e -Adangal application to access the land 
details like Survey No., Sub -Division No., Total extent of land, Classification of land, 
Assessment of Land, Name of the Owner, etc.

Special Refinance Schemes  
1. Transformation of PACS as MSC 
Primary Agricultural Cooperative Credit Societies (PACS) are grass root level Cooperative 
institutions primarily involved in meeting the credit requirement of the farmer members. 
There is a felt need to develop PACS as Multi Service Centres (MSC) for meeti ng credit plus 
requirements of the members and also to enable the societies to diversify their business and 
act as one stop shop for requirements of its members.  
To develop PACS into MSC, a Special Refinance Scheme (SRS) was introduced by NABARD at 
concessional ROI of just 3% to StCBs for providing assistance to PACS through DCCBs. In 
Tamil Nadu TNStCB provided the concessional funding to PACS at 4% p.a through DCCBs. In 
convergence with GoI interest subvention scheme of Agri Infrastructure Fund (AIF ) at PACS 
level the ROI was just 1% p.a. Further, NABARD provides for need based grant component of 
10% of loan amount or ₹2.00 lakh whichever is lesser to eligible PACS  towards managerial 
support, capacity building of members and PACS & brand promotion and market promotion. 
Under the above scheme so far 4599 projects involving 2050 PACS with total project cost of 
₹384.16 crore have been sanctioned in Tamil Nadu. Concessional refinance to the extent of 
₹347.29 crore has been provided by NABARD. PACS under the scheme have been earning 
additional annual income in the range of ₹2 lakh to ₹16 lakh. Additional services undertaken 
by PACS include Custom Hiring Centres, godowns, mini oil mills, rural haats, mini food 
processing units, farmers markets, agri drones etc.

The state is endowed with native breeds of cattle such as Kangeyam (Tiruppur, Erode, 
Coimbatore and Karur districts), Umbalachery (Thanjavur, Tiruvarur, Nagapattinam and 
Cuddalore districts), Alambadi (Dharmapuri, Erode and Salem districts), Pulikulam

(The Nilgiris district). Apart from these native cattle breeds, high milk yielding cross bred of 
Jersey (in plains) and Holstein Friesian (in hills) are being reared extensively by farmers. 
3.6.6.3 Animal Husbandry – Poultry: 
The Potential in the sector is due to a combination of factors - growth in per capita income, a 
growing urban population and falling real poultry prices. Poultry sector in India can be broadly 
divided into two sub-sectors – one with a highly organized commercial sector with about 80% 
of the total market share and the other being unorganized with about 20% of the total market 
share.  
Poultry farming has undergone a transformation from being mere backyard avocation to the 
present vibrant and dynamic commercial enterprise in Tamil Nadu. Poultry rearing is a 
commercial activity prominent in the districts of Namakkal, Salem, Erode and Coim batore. 
Namakkal belt continues to be the egg basket of the State contributing around 65% of the total 
egg production. The State ranks 1st in respect of poultry with 120.78 million poultry and ranks 
second in egg production, 21560.66 Million number of eggs. The per capita availability of egg 
is 281 nos./year against the ICMR recommendations of 180 nos. of eggs/year.

3.6.7 Fisheries  
Tamil Nadu is a leading State with Marine, Inland and Coastal waters with rich biodiversity of 
aquatic fauna and flora. The sector plays an important role in the socio - economic 
development of the state by providing livelihood to a large number of fishers and fish farmers, 
generating employment opportunities in allied sectors and ensuring nutritional security. 
During 2022-23, the sector contributed 6.26% to the State's agricultural GDP. Tamil Nadu 
stands at 5th in marine fish production in the country with a total fish production of 8.29 lakh 
tonnes. The fisheries sector contributed ₹6,957.67 crore to foreign exchange earnings by 
exporting 1.23 lakh tonnes of fish and related products during the period (Fisheries Policy

supports the livelihood of 10.48 lakh marine fishers living in 608 Fish ing villages. There are 
5440 mechanized and 44,487 traditional fishing crafts actively engaged in fishing. Further, 
promotion of mariculture enables the fisher folk to switch over from the concept of only 
capturing the marine resources to diversification i nto stocking and harvesting. (Fisheries

3.6.9 Climate Change – Adaptation and Mitigation 
Climate Change is an undisputed reality causing severe impact on the natural environment, 
human lives, economic assets and activities thus posing an urgent need for comprehensive 
climate action. GoTN places significant importance on addressing climate change, recognizing 
it as a major challenge that threatens the state's environmental, economic, and social well -
being. The state has adopted a proactive approach to mitigate and adapt to the impacts of 
climate change through various policies, plans, and initiatives. 
3.6.9.1 Tamil Nadu State Action Plan on Climate Change (TNSAPCC): 
The TNSAPCC, launched in 2015, is a comprehensive framework. It provided the first State -
wide and cross sectoral climate change impact and vulnerability assessment. The plan also 
formulated a range of adaptation and mitigation strategies to be implemented by various 
Departments, showcasing the state's commitment to combat climate change. To reiterate its 
commitment to addressing the critical issue of climate change, the GoTN has prepared the 
second edition of the State Action Plan on Climate Change (TNSAPCC 2.0) for the years 2022-
2030. 
The action plan has identified the following eleven vulnerable sectors, viz., 
1. Sustainable Agriculture & Allied Sectors 
2. Water Resources 
3. Forests & Biodiversity 
4. Coastal Area Management 
5. Strategic Knowledge and Climate Literacy 
6. Children and Youth for Climate Action 
7. Disaster Management and Mitigation 
8. Health and Sanitation 
9. Sustainable Habitat 
10. Enhanced Energy Efficiency & Solar Mission 
11. Gender and Climate Change 
3.6.9.2 District Climate Change Mission (DCCM):  
For the first time in the Country, the GoTN has set up DCCM with the District Collector as the 
Mission Director and the District Forest Officer as the District Climate Officer to strengthen 
the climate response at the grassroots level. The objectives of the DCCM are to: 
1) work with all Departments at the District level in line with the State Action Plan. 
2) closely associate itself with the Project Management Unit of the Tamil Nadu Green Climate 
Company (TNGCC).

3.7.2.1 Skill Development 
The objective of the National Policy on Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, 2015 is to 
meet the challenge of skilling with speed and standard (quality). It aims to provide an umbrella 
framework to all skilled activities being carried out within the cou ntry, to align them to 
common standards and link the skilling with demand centres. The objective of this skill 
certification and reward scheme is to enable and mobilize a large number of Indian youths to 
take up outcome-based skill training and become employable and earn their livelihood.  
Under Skill India Mission, Skill Development Ministry is implementing Pradhan Mantri 
Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) 2016 -20 to impart Short Term Training (STT) and 
Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) on pan -India basis including State of Tamil Nadu 
covering all districts. 
The Make in India Programme is designed to facilitate investment, foster innovation, protect 
intellectual property and build best -in-class manufacturing infrastructure. The Skill India 
Programme complements the Make in India Programme of the GoI. 
3.7.2.2 Tamil Nadu Skill Development Corporation 
Tamil Nadu Skill Development Corporation is the State Nodal Agency for Skill Development 
whose vision is to transform the state into skill hub by skilling the youth to enhance their 
employability and match the expectations of the Industry. The agency imple ments the 
following State and Central Government Schemes: 
1. Short Term Skill Training (STT) 
TNSDC actively collaborates with Government Agencies, reputed private skill training 
institutions and industry partners to impart industry oriented and placement linked skill 
training. Under this scheme candidates can register in TNSDC portal for free training offered 
by TNSDC. Trainees will be assessed & certified by State Council for Vocational Training 
(SCVT)/ Sector Skill Council (SSC) or any other reputed agency as decided by TNSDC. 
2. Skill Certification Under Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) 
Recognition of Prior Learning commonly known as RPL refers to an assessment process used 
to evaluate a person’s existing skill sets, knowledge and experience gained either by formal, 
non-formal or informal learning. It aims to align the competencies of the un -regulated 
workforce of the country to the standardized National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF). 
3. MSME Skill Training and Employment Scheme 
In order to  ensure supply of quality workforce to the MSME sector, candidates were given 
intensive training under MSME Skill Training and Employment Scheme in the MSME units 
for which a monthly stipend of ₹2000/- per candidate is being paid by TNSDC.

2.0. The scheme is being implemented from March 2018 onwards through 160 approved 
Training Partners and 385 Training Centres. As on December 2019, a total number of 41,991

3.9 Micro Credit 
3.9.1 SHG – Bank Linkage Programme  
The Self -Help Group (SHG)–Bank Linkage Programme (BLP) has emerged as a globally 
recognized microfinance model, fostering financial inclusion and empowering marginalized 
communities. As of March 2024, SHGs in TN reported a savings balance of ₹2854.39 crore 
and credit outstanding of ₹21766.63 crore. With 90% of these groups being women-led, SHG-
BLP has shattered myths about the “non -bankability” of the poor. However, the state’s SHG 
NPAs are at 6.67%, much higher than the national average of 2.05%. NABARD’s capacity -
building initiatives aim to address this concern. 
3.9.2 SHG –BLP - NRLM  
National Rural Livelihood Mission (NRLM), a programme of GoI, is implemented in Tamil 
Nadu as TNSRLM by TNCDW. TNSRLM envisages creation of sustainable livelihoods of the 
rural poor living below the poverty line within a period of 5 to 7 years in all the r ural districts 
of Tamil Nadu. Under the programme Village Poverty Reduction Committees are established 
which is an independent body of the target poor. They are the important link between the 
Project and the Village Community, who are responsible for imple menting the Project at the 
village level. Further, SHG federations are formed and strengthened at the panchayat 
level, called Panchayat Level Federations (PLFs) with the representation from target 
communities. Panchayat Level Federations have been promoted  as the Community Based 
Organisations to strengthen and lead the SHGs by providing various financial and other 
services. These PLFs are restructured and registered under Tamil Nadu Societies Registration 
Act, 1975. The PLFs provide a common platform  for th e SHGs for their economic 
empowerment and act as custodians of SHGs. Any poverty alleviation project fund is routed 
through PLF to the target poor. The office bearers of the PLF shall operate the financial 
transaction of project fund. PLFs are availing bulk loan ranging from 10 lakhs to 3 crores from 
banks for onlending to SHG members, to fill the gap in financing made by the Banks.  
3.9.3 Micro Enterprise Development Programme (MEDP) & Livelihood and 
Enterprise Development Programme (LEDP)  
NABARD supports SHG skill -building via the Micro Enterprise Development Programme 
(MEDP) and Livelihood and Enterprise Development Programme (LEDP), offering training 
in diverse fields like food processing, embroidery, livestock farming, and handicrafts. Between 
2018 and 2024, 290 MEDPs were sanctioned with NABARD assistance of ₹242.9 lakhs.  
NABARD supports the m-Suwidha scheme, a DPR mode project, to enhance the capacities & 
income levels of SHGs and JLGs by identifying skill gaps and promoting sustainable micro -
enterprises with credit support from banks. The scheme aims to establish at least 500 micro-
enterprises through a cluster approach, facilitating collaboration with sector experts fostering 
economic empowerment for women.

3.12 Sustainable Agriculture Practices 
3.12.1 Initiatives of State Government: The State Government is aiming at achieving the 
Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) before 2030 by implementing various schemes. To 
restore water related ecosystem, to give importance for rainwater harvesting and to implement 
the water resource management is the 6 th goal of SDGs, the following soil and water 
conservation and water management schemes are implemented. 
1. Kalaignarin All Village Integrated Agricultural Development Programme 
In the past three years, this scheme was implemented in 7,705 villages throughout Tamil 
Nadu. Under the component, creation of water source for dryland clusters, so far, 916 wells 
have been newly created and installation of Electric/ Solar powered pumpsets  is being done. 
For the creation of water source for Individual SC/ST – small and marginal farmers, so far 
1,306 wells have been newly created. To harvest the rainwater in their own land by farmers, 
so far 1,759 farm ponds were created. Under the component  of rehabilitation  and 
improvement works in panchayat union minor irrigation tanks, ooranies, ponds, supply 
channels and other water harvesting structure- 5,731 have been desilted so far. 
2. Creation and maintenance of water harvesting structures 
In order to overcome the water scarcity by way of increasing the ground water level by 
harvesting the runoff rain water, from the year 2021-22, maintenance works have been carried 
out in the already constructed 2,505 structures. During the current year, 10 0 new water 
harvesting structures like community ponds are to be created besides taking up maintenance 
works in 500 existing water harvesting structures created in various watersheds.  
3. Special Area Development Programme 
For conserving the natural resources of hilly areas, soil and water conservation works and land 
development works are being implemented in the Western Ghat areas and its forest fringe 
villages, under Special Area Development Programme, thereby benefitting the agricultural 
lands. Under this scheme, totally 153 Nos. and 12,971 metres of soil and water conservation 
and land development works have been carried out during the year 2023-24 at a cost of ₹16.24 
crore in the 11 districts.

3.12.2 Initiatives by NABARD 
1. Watershed Development initiatives  
NABARD’s participatory watershed development programme  is being implemented in 
rainfed/dryland areas with major objectives of conservation of soil and water resources, 
enhancement of farm production, productivity and farmers’ income and improvement in 
overall socio-economic status of farmers, women and landle ss labourers. The programme is 
implemented with ‘Ridge to Valley approach’ by treating each and every piece of land for in -
situ soil and water conservation through a process of participatory net planning involving

7. Tribal Development 
The tribal communities are dependent mainly on agriculture, forests and livestock for 
livelihood. But, the dwindling forest resources, accentuated by primitive agriculture practices 
like shifting cultivation, mono -cropping, etc., have jeopardized the agric ulture and livestock 
productivity and led to shrinking water resources and reduced fuel & fodder supply. This has 
largely affected family income leading to rampant migration to urban areas leaving their 
productive assets idle. In many parts of the country,  the tribal communities reside in 
inaccessible areas and are still devoid of common infrastructure facilities such as roads and 
communication, health and education and safe drinking water, which do not allow them to 
absorb technological and financial facilities, being provided by the government. 
The model of tribal development conceived by NABARD encompasses Natural Resource 
Management in rain-fed tribal areas, microfinance initiatives and women upliftment through 
people participation. 
NABARD has sanctioned 30 Tribal Development Fund (TDF) Projects to various Project 
Implementing Agencies (PIAs). Under these TDF projects various activities like ensuring 
plantation in 0.5 to 1.0 acre wadi area, Water resources Development & Soil Conservat ion 
activities, Livelihood activities for landless families, Capacity building/awareness 
programs/training programs etc., Community health and women development are 
undertaken.

weedicides and genetically engineered crops.

Tamil Nadu constitutes 4 percent of India’s land area and is inhabited by 6 percent of India’s 
population but has only 3 percent of India’s water resources. More than 95 percent of the 
surface water and 80 percent of the ground water have already been put into use. Major uses 
of water include human/animal consumption, irrigation and industrial use. The per capita 
availability of water resources, however, is just 900 cubic meters when compared to the 
national average of 2,200 cubic meters. Agriculture is the  largest consumer of water in the 
State using 75 per cent of the State’s water resources. (www.tnenvis.nic.in). The State is 
largely dependent on both the monsoons. The annual average rainfall is around 990 mm (47% 
during the north-east monsoon, 35% during the south-west monsoon, 14% in the summer and 
4% in the winter). Since the State is entirely dependent on rains  for recharging its water 
resources, monsoon failures lead to acute water scarcity and severe droughts. Hence taking 
appropriate measures to arrest the alarmingly decreasing levels of ground water viz. usage of 
water harvesting systems and micro irrigation systems are essential.   
There are 34 Rivers in the State which have been grouped into 17 major River Basins and 127 
Sub-Basins. Cauvery is the only major basin. Of the others, 13 basins are medium and 3 are 
minor river basins.  The annual surface water generated within the State is 692.78 TMC 
(19,619 MCM). The State depends on neighboring States (Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and 
Kerala) for considerable quantum of flows, which is about 261.70 TMC (7411 MCM) annually.

Farm Mechanization is one of the technological inputs that is required to improve the process 
which can transform the subsistence farming to commercial farming. It has the potential to 
expand production, improve timeliness of operations, better utilization of irrigation potential 
and infrastructure, compensate for labour shortages, and alleviate drudgery in agricultural 
operations. Thus, farm mechanization brings about significant improvement in agricultural 
productivity, which underscores the strong need for mechanization of agricultural operations. 
Keeping this in view, an ambitious target of increasing the availability of farm power from 2.02 
kW per ha (2016 -17) to 4.0 kW per ha by the end of 2030 has been set for the country. The 
average farm power avail ability in the state of Tamil Nadu is 1.50 kW/ha, which is mainly 
restricted to tillage operations. This needs to be increased to at least 2 kW/ha as envisaged 
under the GoI’s Sub -Mission on Agricultural Mechanization (SMAM), to increase farm 
income. Post-harvest machinery also helps in value addition and conservation of produce and 
by-products from qualitative and quantitative damages.

geographical area of 130.05 lakh Ha, horticulture crops are cultivated in 16.03 lakh Ha, with a

Tamil Nadu. Under plantation crops, coconut (65%), cashew (12%) and tea (9%) are the 
leading plantation crops in Tamil Nadu. (Source: Agriculture Policy Note, 2024 -25). Off -
season production of mango and round the year production of grapes is unique to Tamil Nadu.

Forests as a life support system play a very crucial role in the ecological stability and economic 
security. The national goal is to have a minimum of one -third of the total land area of the 
country under forest or tree cover. In the hills and in mountaino us regions, the aim is to 
maintain two -third of the area under such cover in order to prevent erosion and land 
degradation and to ensure the stability of the fragile eco -system. Social forestry and 
agroforestry are also advocated to address the present cha llenges of food, nutrition, energy, 
employment and environmental security.  
In consonance with National Forest Policy, GoTN has formulated its State Forest Policy 2018 
with specific emphasis on the following: (1) Nurturing a rich heritage and preserving ecology 
of distinct geographical characteristics of the State, (2) Enhancing t he forest and tree cover, 
(3) Enriching wildlife habitats on scientific principles, without sacrificing the livelihood needs 
of the local communities specially the tribal communities and other forest dwellers.  
As per the latest India’s State of Forest Report, 2023 (Biennial), based on the interpretation of 
Indian Remote Sensing Resourcesat -2 LISS III satellite data of the period Oct 2017 to Aug 
2018, the Forest Cover in the State is 26,450.22 sq km which is 20.3 4% of the State's 
geographical area. In terms of forest canopy density classes, the State has 3,586.19 sq.km of 
very dense forest (VDF) (2.76 % of geographical area), 11,027.03 sq.km of moderately dense 
forest (MDF) (8.48% of geographical area) and 11,837 sq.km of open forest (9.10 % of 
geographical area). The State has constituted Biodiversity Board to manage the key 
biodiversity resources in the State. The State also has Wetland Authority to guide, monitor and 
regulate the management of wetlands. Further, there is an emphasis on agro-forestry and tree-
crop plantations.

capacity is predominantly managed by three public agencies viz., Food C orporation of India

essential for public distribution systems and various government initiatives, thereby limiting 
available space for private stakeholders to store their agricultural produce.

the welfare of both groups. Therefore, addressing the infrastructure needs for storage and 
marketing should be prioritized. The Government of India has introduced several credit -
linked schemes, such as the Agricultural Marketing Infrastructure (AMI) Scheme and the 
Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF), aimed at boosting the development of post -harvest 
facilities and primary processing infrastructure. Under these sch emes, financial assistance is 
provided for constructing or renovating warehouses in rural areas, with subsidies ranging 
from 25% to 33.33% of the project's capital cost depending on the beneficiary category.

The Food and Agro-Processing sector in Tamil Nadu encompasses the transformation of raw 
material from various agricultural sources including food grains, horticultural and plantation

pivotal in preserving food, generating employment, and boosting export revenues.

Agri Business has initiated measures to reduce post-harvest losses and increase the processing 
of fruits and vegetables from the current 2% to 10%. Under the Pradhan Mantri Kisan 
SAMPADA Yojana (PMKSY), eight agro -processing clusters are being established with an 
investment of ₹218 crore in the districts of Theni, Dindigul, Krishnagiri, Tiruvannamalai,

capabilities and benefit farmers in adjacent areas. (Source: Ministry of Food Processing

the state has introduced the Tamil Nadu Food Processing Policy 2018. This policy encourages 
investments, innovation, and job creation in the food processing sector . (Source: NSWS, 
Tamil Nadu Food Processing Policy-2018.pdf). Additionally, the Tamil Nadu Food Processing 
and Agri Export Promotion Corporation (TNAPEx) has been established to propel the state's 
agricultural and food processing sectors towards global prominence by fostering innovation, 
sustainability, and market-driven strategies. (Source: TNApex) 
The Government of India's Pradhan Mantri Formalisation of Micro Food Processing 
Enterprises (PMFME) Scheme, launched in June 2020, is a centrally sponsored initiative 
under the Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan. With an outlay of ₹10,000 crore for the period FY 
2020-2025, now extended to FY 2025-26, the scheme aims to enhance the competitiveness of 
existing individual micro-enterprises in the unorganized food processing sector and promote 
its formalization. The PMFME Scheme provides a 35% credit -linked capital sub sidy to food 
processing entrepreneurs, with a maximum ceiling of ₹10 lakh per unit. It also offers seed 
capital of ₹40,000 per Self Help Group (SHG) member for working capital and the purchase 
of small tools. Furthermore, the scheme provides a 50% financia l grant for branding and 
marketing support to groups such as Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs), SHGs, 
cooperatives, or Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) of micro food processing enterprises. 
(Source: PMFME)

Tamil Nadu stands as a significant contributor to India's MSME landscape. As of March 2024,

development projects and enacted the Real Estate (Regulation and Develop ment) Bill, 2013, 
alongside establishing an Urban Housing Fund. As of 2024, Tamil Nadu has made significant

houses completed, addressing the housing needs of rural communi ties. PMAY (Urban) has 
also facilitated affordable housing in urban areas, with Tamil Nadu ranking among the top -
performing states in implementing the scheme.

5.1 Background
A co-operative is defined as ‘an autonomous association of persons united voluntarily to meet 
their common social, economic and cultural needs as well as their aspirations through a jointly 
owned and democratically controlled enterprise’. 
A co-operative is governed by seven major principles, i.e. voluntary and open membership; 
principle of democratic member control; principle of member economic participation; 
principle of autonomy and independence; principle of education, training and information; 
principle of co-operation and principle of concern for community. 
Co-operative enterprises help their members to collectively solve shared socio -economic 
problems. Co-operatives strengthen bargaining powers of their members, help them get access 
to competitive markets and to capitalise on new market opportunities. As such, they improve 
income opportunities, reduce costs and manage risks of the members.

A Digital Transformation for Rural Finance: The PACS Computerization 
Project in Tamil Nadu 
The Ministry of Cooperation, Government of India, in collaboration with State 
Governments, NABARD, National Federations, training establishments, and other 
stakeholders, has launched the ‘Computerization of Primary Agriculture Cooperative 
Societies’ (CSPCP) project. This initiative aims to computerize 63,000 functional PACS 
across the country, enhancing their operational efficiency, profitability, transparency, and 
accountability. The total project cost is ₹2,516 Crore, with NABARD contributing 10% of the 
total cost. This includes the development of comprehensive software, which covers cyber 
security, data storage, and training for PACS officials. 
NABARD plays a crucial role in the implementation, monitoring, ERP software 
development, and providing capacity -building training for PACS officials, ensuring the 
seamless integration of technology into cooperative societies. The project’s successful 
completion will bring numerous benefits, including streamlined operations, better financial 
management, and improved transparency in transactions. 
In Tamil Nadu, 4,532 PACS have been identified for this project, with a total project cost of 
₹195 Crore dedicated to computerizing these societies. As of now, 4,528 PACS in Tamil 
Nadu are already operating under the e-PACS software, marking significant progress in the 
region.

Introduction
Improvement of rural infrastructure is critical in increasing the competitiveness of the rural 
areas and their incomes.  Several studies show the linkage between infrastructure, poverty 
reduction, improved livelihoods and holistic development of the people . NABARD has been 
partnering with GoTN for meeting the above goals by extending support for creation of 
infrastructure in Agriculture, Social and Rural Connectivity Sectors. 
Rural infrastructure refers to a wide array of physical infrastructure, including energy and 
transport equipment, information and communications technologies, water and sanitation 
facilities, irrigation systems, and market and storage facilities. Rural inf rastructure projects 
are for the essential facilities and services to meet public health and environmental standards 
and to aid the development of trade, commerce, industry, agriculture, aquaculture, and 
employment opportunities. Rural infrastructure is also defined as the basic facilities, services, 
and installations needed for the functioning of a community or society. 
Setting up infrastructure in rural areas has certain challenges like reduced economies of scale, 
higher unit costs, lower incomes, challenges related to pricing of services and there by 
challenging the willingness of private sector participation. In such a  crucial situation, 
Government has to fill up the gap. Ideally, more contribution from the private sector would 
help in addressing the rural infrastructure shortcomings. 
The State’s Vision towards $1 Trillion Economy by 2030 lays out the roadmap for building 
robust infrastructure, skilled human capital, and a thriving innovation ecosystem to serve as 
catalysts, propelling Tamil Nadu swiftly towards its ambitious $1 Trillio n vision. This vision 
calls for setting up of robust support infrastructure for planning, production, processing, 
storage, distribution, marketing and sales of agricultural produce. 
Major infrastructure gaps identified in rural areas of Tamil Nadu, as per the need and demand 
of rural population are irrigation, roads and bridges which are essential to connect isolated 
communities, agriculture and related infrastructure, power supply, e ducation, skilling etc. 
Plugging these gaps will ignite rural activities and create ample economic and employment 
opportunities. 
Tamil Nadu is a water starved state. Only 58 % of the net cultivated area is under irrigated 
agriculture. The efforts of State Government is towards increasing the farm productivity of 
crops through effective water use. Due to seasonal and erratic rainfall in terms of timing and 
geographical distributi on, irrigation is critical for successful agricultural operations in the 
State. The per capita water potential of Tamil Nadu is less than the country’s average. It has 
almost fully developed its surface water potential and rapidly reaching the limit of exploitation 
of its ground water resources. Further, rising sea levels due to climate change has resulted in 
intrusion of sea water into freshwater courses which meet the irrigation needs of several area 
of ayacut in the coastal regions. Consequently, future expansion of irrigated agriculture in 
Tamil Nadu depends largely on conservation of available water and achieving greater 
efficiency of water use in the existing systems.

Climate change is affecting every region on  the Earth, in multiple ways. The IPCC AR6[]  
highlights that human-induced climate change is intensifying weather and climate extremes, 
resulting in unprecedented heatwaves, heavy rainfall, and severe  droughts. The frequency 
and intensity of these events are  likely to increase, posing significant risks to ecosystems, 
biodiversity, and human societies.
India is exposed to a whole range of climate and weather-related hazards. India with 
diverse geographical regions,  long coastline, biodiversity, and high dependence on natural 
resources is one of the most vulnerable countries to climate change risks worldwide. Further, 
more than half of India’s population lives in rural areas and depends on agriculture  & allied 
activities, which are highly sensitive to climate change, threatening the livelihoods of people 
dependent on them. 
There is emerging evidence that the  productivity of crops, livestock and fish is likely to be 
affected with implications to food security, livelihoods, and sustainability in agriculture.  In 
India, several studies have projected declining crop  yields, in the absence of adaptation to 
climate change. As per the district level risk  and vulnerability assessment of Indian   
agriculture to climate change undertaken by ICAR-CRIDA, 109 districts out of 573 rural 
districts (19% of total districts) are ‘very high-risk’ districts, while 201 districts are high -risk 
districts. Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change 
(IPCC), 2022 ICAR-CRIDA (2019): Risk and Vulnerability Assessment of Indian Agriculture 
to Climate Change. 
Climate finance requirement of India is enormous. While the preliminary financial estimates 
for meeting India’s climate change actions as per NDC was USD 2.5 trillion between 2015 and 
2030, estimated financial requirement of India to become net-zero by 2070 as per IFC is 
US$10.1 trillion. There are various estimates of financial requirements that vary greatly due 
to varying levels of detail, but it is important to note that they all point to a need for tens of 
trillions of US dollars. India’s updated NDCs also indicates the need to better adapt to climate 
change by enhancing investments in development programmes in sectors vulnerable to  
climate change, however financial requirements for adaptation are very large and will increase 
in the future. To fully meet our NDCs in a timely manner, India requires enhanced new and 
additional financial, technological and capacity building support. However, financial,  and 
technological commitments by developed countries under the Paris Agreement are yet to be 
fully transpired. 
India initiated the National Action Plan  on Climate Change (NAPCC) in 2008, which 
introduced eight National  Missions encompassing  various efforts. In August 2022, the 
Government of India displayed greater determination in its efforts to address climate change 
by submitting its revised Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) to the UNFCCC. Through 
Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for the Environment), India advocated for a global shift in mindset 
and behaviour, moving away from thoughtless and harmful consumption towards purposeful 
and conscious utilisation.
